title: A sensitivity bar chart asks which few reactions control the answer, and whether that list changes with temperature
summary: Each bar is how strongly the ignition delay responds to a small change in one reaction's rate. Long bars are the reactions worth tuning, bars inside the dashed 5 percent lines are dropped, and comparing two temperatures shows that the controlling reactions are different in different regimes.

media.alt: Horizontal bar chart titled Sensitivity Analysis for n-heptane. Reaction identifiers run down the y axis, sensitivity coefficients run along the x axis from about minus 0.25 to plus 0.25. Red bars (900 K) are long, reaching from minus 0.2 to plus 0.22. Blue bars (1200 K) are barely visible. Two vertical dashed lines mark the 5 percent threshold on each side of zero.

read_the_figure.question: Which reactions does the ignition delay depend on most, at each of the two temperatures, and which can be left alone?
read_the_figure.axes: y: reaction identifiers in mechanism order, sorted from the largest absolute sensitivity at the top. x: first-order sensitivity coefficient, symmetric about zero. Red bars: the lower of the two temperatures (850 K for methyl butanoate, 900 K for n-heptane). Blue bars: 1200 K. Dashed lines: the 5 percent selection threshold on each side.
look_at: Bars outside the dashed lines are the reactions that pass the threshold. Count them: that count is the number of parameters the later optimization or response surface has to handle.
Sign. A bar to the left of zero means increasing that reaction's rate reduces the ignition delay (faster ignition). A bar to the right means the opposite.
Colour contrast. In the low-temperature charts the red bars are long and the blue bars are close to zero. The reactions that control ignition near 850 or 900 K barely matter at 1200 K.
The sort order is by size, so the shape of the lower half tells you how fast the tail decays. A long tail of small bars means many weak contributors.

The four figures in the group are two fuels by two temperature regimes. The high-temperature charts (03 and 05) select a different set of reactions from the low-temperature charts (02 and 04), which is why they are separate figures.
read_the_figure.proves: That a small, identifiable subset of the reaction rates dominates the response at each regime. It does not prove those rates are the ones that are wrong, only that they are the ones that matter if they are.
if_wrong: All bars short: the observable is insensitive to these parameters, or the perturbation size was too small to see above numerical noise.
A bar just outside the threshold at one temperature and inside at the other: the selection is temperature-dependent, so a single list for all conditions needs a union.
Large bars of opposite sign for chemically similar reactions: compensation. The data cannot separate them and tuning one will be traded against the other.
must_check: The normalisation of the coefficient is stated (it is not on these axes).
The perturbation size used for the derivative and that the result does not depend on it.
Both temperatures drawn on the same x range, so bar lengths are comparable.
The threshold is stated, and the reason for 5 percent.
The observable is named (here the title says sensitivity analysis and the caption speaks of ignition delay targets).

terms.meaning: How much the output changes, to first order, when one input is changed on its own, others held at nominal.
Sensitivity of the logarithm of the output to the logarithm of the input. It is a dimensionless percent-per-percent measure.
A cut-off on the absolute sensitivity. Inputs below it are fixed at nominal and treated as inactive.
An input that passes the threshold and is allowed to vary in the optimization or the surrogate model.
Two regimes of the ignition mechanism. At low temperature, peroxy and isomerisation steps dominate. At high temperature, small-radical chain branching dominates.
An estimate of a derivative from two runs with a small change of the input.
Perturbing a single input per run. It misses interaction effects between inputs.

remember: Sensitivity is local: it describes the neighbourhood of the nominal parameters.
The sign says direction, the length says importance.
The set of important reactions changes with temperature regime.
A threshold turns a ranking into a selection, and the selection decides how big the next problem is.

steps.title: Define the normalised coefficient
steps.note: A coefficient of -0.1 means a 10 percent increase of the rate shortens the delay by about 1 percent. Dimensionless, so reactions with very different rate magnitudes can share one axis.

steps.title: Estimate it from two runs
steps.note: Run once at nominal and once with one rate scaled by a small factor. The perturbation must be small enough for the response to be linear but large enough to be above solver tolerance.

steps.title: Why the coefficient is a first-order Taylor term
steps.note: This is the model behind the bar chart: if every reaction rate moves by a factor, the log delay moves by the weighted sum. It breaks down for large perturbations and when interactions matter.

steps.title: The selection rule
steps.note: The reactions to keep are those whose bar crosses either dashed line. The figure draws theta as 5 percent. If a reaction passes at either temperature it is kept, so the union is larger than either set.

steps.title: Why the sign matters for tuning
steps.note: To make a mechanism ignite faster you increase rates with negative bars and decrease rates with positive bars. Two reactions with opposite signs and equal sizes can offset each other, and that is where the data cannot decide between them.

steps.title: Linear combination of two parameters
steps.note: Valid only for small changes. If two bars are large and of opposite sign the effect of changing both depends on their interaction, which this chart cannot show.

worked.title: Reading a sensitivity from two runs
worked.problem: Scaling one rate by 1.10 shortens the ignition delay from 1.00 ms to 0.95 ms. What is the normalised first-order sensitivity, and does it pass a 5 percent threshold?

solution.text: Apply the finite-difference formula in logs.

worked.answer: S is about -0.54: this is a strongly controlling reaction (far longer than the bars in the figure, which stay below about 0.25 in magnitude), and it passes any 5 percent threshold. The numbers are a teaching example, not from the figure.

analyze.q: In the low-temperature charts the blue (1200 K) bars are nearly absent. In words, what does that say about which reactions a low-temperature-only optimization can change?
analyze.hint: If a reaction is irrelevant at 1200 K, what happens to the 1200 K predictions when it is tuned?

analyze.q: A reaction has a bar just inside the dashed line at both temperatures. Would you drop it? What would change your mind?
analyze.hint: Interactions, uncertainty size of that rate, how many parameters you can afford.

analyze.q: Why is one-at-a-time sensitivity a risky basis for choosing parameters when two bars have opposite signs?

evaluate.q: Is a fixed 5 percent threshold a good rule for choosing active parameters across two fuels? What alternatives would you compare?
evaluate.hint: Cumulative fraction of total variance; a fixed budget of parameters; using the prior uncertainty of each rate.

evaluate.q: The chart ranks sensitivities but not uncertainties. Why can a high-sensitivity reaction still be a poor tuning candidate?
evaluate.hint: A well-known rate has little room to move.

create: Redraw the chart as a paired bar (blue and red adjacent, same row) with a column for each reaction's prior uncertainty, so the reader can see both how much a rate matters and how much it is allowed to move.
Design a test that checks the first-order assumption: perturb two active reactions together and compare the result with the sum of their separate effects.

checks.q: What does a negative bar mean?
checks.hint: Think of what happens to the ignition delay when that rate goes up.
checks.answer: Increasing that reaction's rate shortens the ignition delay, so ignition becomes faster. A positive bar means the opposite.

checks.q: A rate is increased by 5 percent and the delay drops by 2.5 percent. What is the approximate normalised sensitivity?
checks.hint: Ratio of the two relative changes (small changes).

checks.q: Why do the high-temperature charts select different reactions than the low-temperature charts?
checks.hint: Which chemistry dominates in each regime?
checks.answer: Different elementary steps control the overall rate: low temperature is controlled by peroxy and isomerisation chemistry, high temperature by small-radical chain branching. A reaction that matters in one regime has no leverage in the other.

checks.q: Two reactions have equal-length bars of opposite sign. What does a tuning on ignition delay alone learn about them?
checks.hint: Only their combined effect enters the data.
checks.answer: Only the combination: the data constrain a weighted sum of the two rates, not each rate. The individual values remain undetermined unless another observable separates them.

checks.q: How would you extend this chart to show a second observable such as flame speed?
checks.answer: Add a second panel with the same row order and a shared y axis, one bar per reaction for the flame-speed sensitivity at one condition. Reactions active in both panels are the ones that couple the two kinds of data.
